slides.title: Knowing when an AI answer is wrong
slides.notes: Introduce yourself; the talk is about telling, from what the pipeline did, when its answer is wrong.

slides.title: An answer is worth more with its confidence
slides.notes: In a company the answer alone is not enough. Its confidence decides where it goes: above a threshold it goes out on its own, below it a person reviews it first. Where the threshold sits depends on what a wrong answer costs: a support desk answers routine questions fast, a contract lookup must surface its doubt, a knowledge base must cite its source, so its answer comes with the passage it quotes. The confidences and thresholds here are illustrative, not measured: the AI answers five times per use case, the support desk at 92, 41, 88, 67 and 94 against 70, the contract lookup at 95, 74, 91, 58 and 82 against 90, the knowledge base at 91, 63, 85, 47 and 88 against 80; a green tick above the threshold, a red cross below, and the answer goes out or to a person.

slides.title: The R2C2 task: answer, cite, and say how sure
slides.notes: R2C2 asks exactly this over a movie corpus of two million passages. What we have: the corpus and 64 questions of six types. What we must return for each: the passages that support it, at most 20, and an answer with a confidence from 0 to 100, with its nuggets, each citing one of those passages. Our search reads those passages from about 10 GB of indexes: 6.4 GB of embeddings and 3.4 GB of keyword index.

slides.title: One pipeline serves both subtasks
slides.notes: The model above chooses one tool call per turn, against the passages DB; the orchestrator below checks every claim, keeps the record and rules on the answer. Then Han Solo's first pass, box by box.

slides.title: Han Solo's other passes
slides.notes: The same question, three more times, on a corpus that shrinks: every passage an earlier pass met is withheld. The type and its note never change; what the search finds does, and so do the checks and the answers: Starkiller Base twice, then Ilum twice.

slides.title: The volume of the run
slides.notes: The whole run in numbers: 65 questions, 236 passes. A question costs a median of 65 tool calls, 157 passages retrieved and 0.69 GPU-hours (RTX PRO 6000-equivalent), its passes summed; most questions sit near the median, a few cost several times more. Pass by pass: pass 1 is the cheapest (13 calls, 21 passages); passes 2 to 4 make about 19 calls but retrieve more and more passages, the corpus shrinking under them; pass 4 ran on 41 of the 65 questions (a fourth pass runs unless the last two came back unsure). GPU-hours: allocated, the run took 86 GPU-hours (74 for the 236 submitted passes), from Slurm accounting, each pass tied to its job through the orchestrator's logs. Shown here RTX PRO 6000-equivalent: a pass on the RTX PRO 6000s as allocated; a pass on the A100s priced at its tool calls times the RTX rate per tool call (0.012 GPU-hours), because 84% of their 5 times higher allocation was the pool's configuration (4 A100s held for one pass at a time), not the passes; seconds per tool call, 32 on the RTX against 38 on the A100 (medians). That makes 49 GPU-hours for the 236 passes. On running time alone (no boot or idle time) the median pass costs 0.08, 0.16, 0.20 and 0.20 GPU-hours in passes 1 to 4: the work grows to pass 3 then levels off; pass 4's higher mean here is the end of the run's idle time. No wall time: the configurations varied.

slides.title: From passes to submission
slides.notes: A run reads only what the passes recorded, by a rule. PG-1: pass 1's passages, the one with a kept nugget first. PG-2: the passes grouped by answer, the best group's passages pooled and ranked the same way. AC-1: pass 1's answer, its confidence raised for agreement. AC-2: the most confident submission. AC-3: the submissions summed by answer, capped at 100. One pass sends Starkiller Base; four send Ilum.

slides.title: Passage retrieval (PR): official results
slides.notes: The organisers' official PR scores (direct judgements), nDCG@20 over the 64 scored questions. Pooling the passes, PG-2, is 4th of the 22 PR runs and the single pass, PG-1, 5th; the three above are one team's, hit-u. Question by question PG-2 is higher on 42, the same on 7, lower on 15; Han Solo is one of its largest gains. Why PG-1 trails: its list is pass 1's record, so it is as long as what pass 1 met; on 21 questions pass 1 searched once, got its 10 results and stopped, and 37 lists are under 20. The gain lives there: +0.1104 on the 37 short lists, +0.0167 on the 27 full ones; cut to PG-1's length, PG-2's lead halves to 0.0411. By type, the gain is largest on post-processing-heavy and multi-hop, the two types whose answer is in no single passage, and there PG-2 is the top run of all 22. Said, not shown: the difference of the means is not significant (Tukey HSD p = 0.4854). Q@20 ranks the runs the same way.

slides.title: Answering with confidence (AC): official results
slides.notes: A run, question by question: each bar its confidence, green when right, red when wrong. R_U is the mean of the green bars, R_O one minus the mean of the red ones, HMR their harmonic mean. An absurd trick: answer the one question we are surest of at 100 and every other one deliberately wrong at 0: R_U 1, R_O 1, HMR 1.0000 at accuracy 1/64. Repeat with 4, 16, 32 answers: still 1.0000, whatever the accuracy; with none right at all, still 1.0000. Confidence 50 everywhere gives 0.5000 at any accuracy, here at the median, 0.8125. Our AC-2: 0.4915, below that: our wrong answers kept a mean confidence of 65.4 (Hannibal's 'fava beans' at 100). Among the 25 official runs AC-2 is 6th on accuracy, 0.9219, 13th on HMR; accHMR, accuracy times HMR, puts the tricks at k/64 and every answer wrong at 0, and AC-2 7th.

slides.title: Additional runs: the same passes, new rules
slides.notes: The same four passes, read by two new rules, with no new model call and no new search. Both take the last answer the model itself submitted, never a refusal the format check wrote over it. Longest deliberation: one pass, trusted only if its longest reasoning turn is no longer than the median of the 65 first passes, 989 characters; Han Solo's longest is 1095, so Starkiller Base at 0: wrong, and now harmless. Taken alone, the longest turn ranks wrong answers above right ones with an AUC of 0.707. Independent agreement: four passes, one vote each (0.35 for a pass handed its answer by a fallback), here 2 against 2; the tie goes to the group whose best pass has the most verified entailment, Ilum 1.940 against Starkiller Base 1.903; two passes reached Ilum on their own, so 100. (Pass 2's sum is 0.96077 + 0.94259 = 1.90336: shown 1.903, its scores 0.961 and 0.943.) Neither rule was judged by the organisers: each answer takes the label of the identical answer they judged.

slides.title: Additional runs: updated AC results
slides.notes: Slide 8's four graphs, each submitted run of ours turning into the additional run that reads the same passes differently; neither was sent to the organisers: each answer takes the label of the identical answer they judged. The single pass, BITEM-AC-1 into revised-longest-deliberation: the same answers, every confidence now 100 or 0; Han Solo's wrong Starkiller Base goes from 99 to 0; HMR 0.2719 to 0.6639. The four passes, BITEM-AC-2 into revised-independent-agreement: 39 confidences change and one verdict, Rogue One, wrong at 97, now pass 1's own answer, right at 50; HMR 0.4915 to 0.6985. Among the 25 official runs: longest deliberation 11th on HMR, 7th on accHMR; independent agreement 9th on HMR, 5th on accuracy, 5th on accHMR. By type only multi-hop changes, to 10 of 10. Hannibal's wrong answer goes from 100 to 0.

slides.title: Conclusion and future work
slides.notes: What the results showed: for passages, pooling the four passes is 4th of 22 runs, one pass 5th; for answers as submitted, accuracy is strong (AC-2 6th of 25) and the confidence weak (HMR 13th); the additional runs read the same passes with new rules and give better confidence: independent agreement 5th on accuracy, 9th on HMR, 5th on accHMR; longest deliberation 7th on accHMR. Future work: the gate checks each nugget against its passage, never the answer against the nuggets: Han Solo's nugget was entailed at 0.975, the gate passed at 98, and the planet is Ilum (the orchestrator's only answer-to-nugget test, `_db_nugget_entails_answer`, is a word overlap in a fallback, and it would say yes here: 2 of 5 words). Then an estimator fitted on the signals a pass already records, chosen on synthetic questions and tested once on R2C2's 64. Aggregation is AC-2's lowest rank by question type (6 of 7 right, 7th of 25; six runs got all 7): a count's evidence is split across passes, each withholding what the passes before met; one pass of the same model, asked to gather more proof, would keep it together (four passes cost 4.8 times one pass's calls). Every pass ran Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8: would a smaller or a bigger model change the results? And the benchmark never tests a question whose answer is not in the corpus: a model right on every question scores perfectly by answering everything at 100; eight such questions answered at 100 take its HMR to 0. To take home, first: being accurate and knowing when you're wrong rarely go together. Of the 25 official answer runs, 10 reach accuracy 0.85 and 8 reach HMR 0.70, but only 4 reach both, all from one team (retrank); the thresholds are a reading aid. This is not 'the more accurate, the less calibrated': across the 25 runs Spearman(accuracy, HMR) is 0.14; what holds is that few runs are high on both. Two pairs of runs were submitted twice (BITEM-AC-3 = AC-4, hit-u-AC-2 = AC-3); their dots stand side by side, as on slide 8. Second: each new pass finds relevant passages the earlier ones missed: relevant passages found per question, so far, 8.5, 11.6, 14.4, 15.9 after passes 1 to 4 (each adding 3.0, 2.9, then 1.4 over the 64; pass 4 ran on 41 of them, 2.2 on each); 40 of the 42 questions where pooling (PG-2) beats one pass (PG-1) hold relevant passages only later passes found. Caveats: the counts are lower bounds, since a passage is judged only if some run submitted it; the new passages are as relevant as pass 1's, not more (15% highly relevant in both); about 42% of the nDCG gain fills slots pass 1 left empty, re-ranking adds nothing; the two-run paired test gives p = 0.0002, but the organisers' test over the 22 runs finds no significant difference.
